newsitem.title: USA: Dime Bancorp to focus on five business areas.
newsitem.headline: Dime Bancorp to focus on five business areas.

text.p: Dime Bancorp Inc is focusing on five business areas, each capable of achieving a 15 percent return on equity, as it changes from a traditional thrift, president and chief executive Lawrence Toal told shareholders at the annual meeting here.
It is transforming "to a "high performance" consumer financial services and mortgage banking firm and "super community bank,he said.
The five areas are mortgage banking, consumer financial services, commercial real estate lending, consumer lending and business banking, which Toal called the "newest opportunity."

Toal said in business banking Dime will seek to capitalize on the relationships it has in the communities it serves. He said the cmopany is bringing in experienced managers in business banking and developing a full range of products. "Our goal is not just lending," he said, adding that products and services include lines of credit, cash management, and transaction accounts.

Asked by shareholders about the recent declaration of a $0.04 per share cash dividend on common shares, the first dividend in several years, Toal said the dividend will be considered by directors each quarter.

Toal said the dividend, which will be paid June 16 to shareholders of record May 16, is an initial dividend and the company would like to increase it. He did not make any specific commitment on future payouts and said it would depend among other things on the capital ratio.

He said the dividend, equivalent to a yield of about one percent if annualized, was "in line with similarly situated thrifts." He also said the initial dividend is a positive development because certain institutional investors are prohibited from buying stocks that do not pay dividends.

Answering a query about Dime's lawsuit seeking damages of about $575 million from the U.S. government, general counsel Gene Brooks said "we think it is a substantial claim." But he said there would be a lengthy legal process and appeals could be expected.

In July 1996 the U.S. Supreme Court ruled the U.S. could be held liable for damages as a result of a breach of contracts it had entered into in government-assisted acquisitions of troubled thrifts. A change in accounting rules resulted in many thrifts -- including Anchor Savings, which merged with Dime in 1996 -- going from overcapitalized to undercapitalized overnight.
Brooks noted that so far none of the cases seeking damages has been decided.

In 1996 Dime, the largest thrift in both New York City and New York State, had a 12 percent return on equity after "normalization" for one-time items. Toal said Dime made "solid progress" in 1996 although it is "not yet where it wants to be."
